description: Hello, we are all here to learn and to expand our knowledge. I want this to be an opportunity to make new friends and to have hands on experience, so don't be scared to approach us. We are open to anyone and everyone. Hope to make new memories 😄
summary: Moonbase Kids is a free browser game that trains children aged 7 to 12 to be junior astronauts for the Moon and Mars. It answers the challenge “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” by turning real mission decisions into play. Children build a rocket, steer a probe through real near-Earth asteroids, build a Moon or Mars base, and watch it face a Sun storm. What makes it different is that the game runs on real NASA data: solar flares from NASA DONKI set the Sun weather, asteroids from NeoWs become the targets, and a Fact button shows space stories from NASA’s Astronomy Picture of the Day and Image and Video Library. If NASA cannot be reached, the game uses saved real NASA data and labels it as archive. A helper robot, Cosmo, gives hints. It matters because space feels far away to young learners, and NASA data is written for scientists. Moonbase Kids makes that data playable, safe and fun, with no install.
details:
Moonbase Kids is a free browser game with seven space games for children aged 7 to 12. In Rocket Builder, a child chooses an engine, fuel tank, shield and tools for a Moon or Mars trip, and a failed launch explains why. Then they steer a probe through real near-Earth asteroids in Asteroid Blaster, and test a Moon or Mars base against a Sun storm in Base Builder. Cosmo, a built-in helper robot, gives hints.

The games run on real NASA data. DONKI solar flares set the Sun weather (Stormy, Active or Calm), which changes the games. NeoWs asteroids become the targets. A Fact button shows the Astronomy Picture of the Day and NASA Image and Video Library facts, with a “Read more at NASA” link. If NASA is slow or offline, the game uses saved real NASA data and labels it “NASA archive”, never “live”.

Children practise real mission choices safely, and see that space data is real and fun. It needs no install and no account, and progress stays on the child’s device. What a child types to Cosmo never leaves the device, because Cosmo is not real AI.

We built it with plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one page, NASA open APIs, the Fredoka font, and automated browser tests at phone-size screens. We used Claude (Anthropic) as an AI tool to help build it.

Limits: the game rules are simplified for kids, not real physics. Next: a classroom mode, accessibility options, and testing with children and phones.
